A Signature in the Letterforms

Many medieval manuscripts do not name the person who copied their text. Historians can compare handwriting, but hundreds of pages make small differences difficult to track consistently. A digital method helps researchers organize those comparisons.

Before analysis, each photographed page is cropped straightened and adjusted for contrast.[1] Software locates repeated letters and records features such as the angle of a stem, the height of a loop, and the distance between strokes. Profiles from several pages can reveal whether the same hand appears in books now held by different libraries.[2]

The program does not identify a scribe by reading the words. Instead, it harvests[3] the shapes made while those words were written. The combination of many measurements produce[4] a profile that can be compared with profiles from other pages.

A close match is evidence, not a final verdict. Ink, writing speed, and the condition of a pen can alter a person's letterforms. Researchers therefore examine the digital result alongside dates, materials, and textual clues. By narrowing a large collection to promising comparisons, the method gives historians more time to study the evidence that a number alone cannot explain.[5]
